title: Percentage and Its Applications — Chapter Summary
intro: Percent means 'per hundred'. Because every percentage shares the same denominator, percentages let us compare quantities of very different sizes at a glance. This chapter develops percentage as a language and applies it to the workhorse problems of commercial mathematics — increase / decrease, profit and loss, discount, and simple and compound interest.

branches.label: Conversions
details: x % of A; A as % of B

sections.heading: Percentage — Definition and Conversions
bullets: Percent = fraction with denominator 100; 25 % = 25/100 = 0.25.
Decimal → percent: multiply by 100 (0.6 = 60 %).
Fraction → percent: convert to decimal, then × 100 (1/8 = 12.5 %).
Percent → fraction: write over 100, simplify (60 % = 3/5).
Percentages can exceed 100 % (e.g. growth rates).
x % of A = (x/100) · A. A as % of B = (A/B) · 100 %.

sections.heading: Increase and Decrease Percent
bullets: Percentage change = (NEW − OLD)/OLD · 100 %.
If positive, it's an increase; if negative, a decrease.
Increase: NEW = A · (1 + p/100). Decrease: NEW = A · (1 − p/100).
Successive p % then q %: total factor = (1 + p/100)(1 + q/100); net % = p + q + pq/100.
10 % up + 10 % down ≠ 0 — net 1 % decrease (multiplicative effect).

sections.heading: Profit and Loss
bullets: CP = cost price; SP = selling price.
Profit = SP − CP (when positive); Loss = CP − SP (when SP < CP).
Profit % = Profit/CP · 100 %; Loss % = Loss/CP · 100 %.
Profit / loss percentages are ALWAYS computed on CP.
Given CP and gain %: SP = CP · (1 + gain%/100).
Given SP and gain %: CP = SP / (1 + gain%/100).

sections.heading: Discount
bullets: MP = marked price; SP after discount = MP − discount.
Discount % is computed on MP.
Combined with markup: marker sets MP above CP; discount reduces MP to SP.
Two successive discounts d₁ % and d₂ % are equivalent to a single discount of (d₁ + d₂ − d₁d₂/100) %, NOT (d₁ + d₂) %.

sections.heading: Simple Interest
bullets: SI = P · r · t / 100, with P = principal, r = rate p.a. (in %), t = time in years.
Amount A = P + SI = P · (1 + r·t/100).
Simple interest is FLAT: each year, the same amount is added.
Re-arrangements: P = SI·100/(r·t); r = SI·100/(P·t); t = SI·100/(P·r).

sections.heading: Compound Interest
bullets: Yearly: A = P · (1 + r/100)^t. CI = A − P.
Each period, interest is added to principal — the principal grows.
Sub-annual compounding (n times a year): A = P · (1 + r/(100·n))^(n·t).
Common cases: half-yearly n = 2; quarterly n = 4; monthly n = 12.
More frequent compounding → larger maturity amount.
Two-year shortcut: CI − SI = P · (r/100)^2.

key_takeaways: % means per hundred; convert freely between fractions, decimals and percents.
Use multiplicative factors (1 ± p/100) to apply percentage changes — addition is wrong.
Profit and loss percentages are on CP; discount percentages are on MP.
Simple interest is linear in time; compound interest is exponential.
More frequent compounding increases the maturity amount.
The 2-year shortcut CI − SI = P(r/100)^2 is a fast sanity check.

glossary.definition: A fraction with denominator 100; the symbol % stands for 'per hundred'.
(New − Old)/Old × 100 % — positive for increase, negative for decrease.
The price at which a trader buys an item.
The price at which the item is sold.
The price tag on the item, typically higher than the eventual selling price after discount.
Profit (Loss) expressed as a percentage of CP.
Reduction in marked price; computed as a percentage of MP.
The original sum borrowed or invested.
The interest rate per annum, expressed as a percent.
Duration of the loan / investment, in years.
Interest computed each year on the original principal: SI = Prt/100.
Interest computed on the running principal (which grows each period): CI = A − P with A = P(1 + r/100)^t for yearly compounding.
Compounding more frequently than once a year; A = P(1 + r/(100n))^(nt) with n = periods per year.
